title: The Supreme Court Will Decide on Asylum at the Border
summary:
For almost two years, the Trump administration has blocked asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border and cancelled thousands of waiting cases. Asylum is a legal protection for people who say they face danger at home. Critics say the path for these people is now nearly closed.

Soon, the U.S. Supreme Court will decide if the president can stop asylum on his own, without Congress. The ban began hours after President Trump took office again. Two lower courts have said no, but the ban has mostly stayed in place.

The administration says the ban guards the border from abuse. Crossings fell sharply: fewer than 99,000 people were caught at the Southwest border in fiscal year 2026, down 95% from more than 1.8 million a year under President Biden. Simon Hankinson of the Heritage Foundation said ending the ban 'would be disastrous.'

Critics disagree. Lee Gelernt of the American Civil Liberties Union said the president cannot override protections from Congress. Advocates say denial rates rose to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024. They point to ZG, an Ethiopian man in his 30s who came through Mexico in February 2025 and was ordered this month to Uganda, a country he has never visited. The court will also look at sending migrants to other countries.
why_it_matters: The court's decision will shape who can ask the United States for safety, and that could affect families and classmates in your own community.

background_read: Asylum is a legal way for people to ask a country to protect them because they say they face danger at home.
In the United States, the president and Congress share power over the rules about who can ask for asylum.
Now the Supreme Court must decide whether the president can stop asylum on his own, even though two lower courts have said no.
